Chapter 3: The Exclusion of Black Women and the Limits of Mainstream Feminism
After the Civil War, the women’s movement really started to pick up steam. Suffrage groups were popping up all over the country, and they were drawing in more people, gaining real political influence.
But as the movement became more visible, something else was happening too. It started closing its doors to some of the very women who needed it most. Black women and other women of color were often pushed aside, their stories and struggles barely mentioned, if at all.
Picture a suffrage rally back then—the crowd is mostly white, and the leaders on stage are talking about the rights of “all women.” But, here’s the thing: their idea of “all” was shaped by their own backgrounds. For a lot of these leaders, winning the vote was about getting access to things like education, property, and social respect—privileges tied to middle-class life. Working-class women, immigrants, and especially women of color? Their challenges rarely came up.
But Black women weren’t about to fade quietly into the background. They built their own clubs and organizations—a whole network where their voices mattered. These groups took on issues like education, healthcare, labor rights, and the ongoing fight against racial violence. Sure, mainstream suffrage leaders might have overlooked them, but their work was absolutely crucial for their communities.
Imagine for a moment: a group of women gathered in a church basement, planning how to make local schools better. They’re sharing stories—not just struggles with discrimination, but also moments of hope and resilience. They know their children’s futures are on the line, so they dig in and get to work. Their activism isn’t just about laws or votes; it’s woven into their everyday lives, shaped by what they face as mothers, workers, and neighbors.
Now, while this was happening, a lot of the mainstream suffrage movement was actually making choices that held inequality in place. Especially in the South, some white suffragists tried to win over powerful men by promising to keep segregation and white supremacy intact. They’d argue that giving white women the vote would help “improve” society, completely ignoring Black women’s needs and rights.
This willingness to compromise on race really showed the limits of what mainstream feminism was willing to fight for. For many Black women, it became painfully clear: their freedom couldn’t depend on someone else’s goodwill. They had to fight for it themselves, building alliances and strategies that truly reflected their own lives.
The exclusion of Black women from the suffrage movement wasn’t just a simple mistake or a lack of awareness. It was rooted in deeper patterns of privilege and power—patterns that shaped the movement from the start. The battle for women’s rights has always been tangled up with questions of race and class, and failing to address these left real wounds that lasted for generations.
Still, even in the face of being left out, Black women led the way. Their organizations became training grounds for new leaders. Their ideas and strategies set the stage for future movements. They understood something vital: true freedom isn’t just about casting a ballot. It’s about justice—real justice—in every part of life.
